briefOverview: A symbolic vision contrasts the woman, her royal child, and the dragon, culminating in Satan’s expulsion from heaven and an ensuing earthly persecution of the faithful.
summary: A luminous woman crowned with twelve stars labors to give birth while a seven‑headed dragon waits to devour her child. She bears a male child destined to rule the nations with a rod of iron; the child is caught up to God, and the woman flees to a divinely prepared wilderness refuge for 1,260 days. A war in heaven ensues: Michael and his angels defeat the dragon, who is cast down to earth with his angels. A heavenly proclamation announces that the accuser is overthrown, and that believers conquer him by the Lamb’s blood, their testimony, and their willingness to face death. Enraged and knowing his time is short, the dragon persecutes the woman; she receives eagle’s wings to reach safety, the earth swallows a flood sent against her, and the dragon turns to wage war on her offspring—those who keep God’s commands and hold the testimony of Jesus.
externalContext: Revelation is apocalyptic literature, a genre that communicates divine truth through symbols, visions, and cosmic conflict imagery familiar in Second Temple Jewish writings. Many interpreters date the book to the late first century CE and situate its original audience among churches in Roman Asia Minor under social and sometimes political pressure. The period of 1,260 days (also expressed as 42 months or “a time, times, and half a time”) commonly functions in Jewish apocalyptic as a limited span of tribulation. Michael is portrayed in Jewish tradition (especially Daniel) as a chief angel and protector of Israel. The wilderness motif evokes Israel’s past experiences of divine protection and provision away from hostile powers.
externalReferences: The child’s destiny to “rule all nations with a rod of iron” echoes Psalm 2:9, a royal-Messianic text applied to Christ in the New Testament. Michael’s role and the time designation “a time, times, and half a time” resonate with Daniel’s visions (Daniel 10:13; 12:1; 7:25; 12:7). The dragon identified as “that ancient serpent” recalls Genesis 3 and the portrayal of Satan as accuser in Job 1:9–11 and Zechariah 3:1–2. The woman’s rescue on “wings of a great eagle” and wilderness sustenance recall Exodus 19:4 and Deuteronomy 32:11, while Satan’s fall aligns with Jesus’ words in Luke 10:18 and the Johannine theme of judgment in John 12:31.
practicalQuestions: What practices help me bear faithful testimony to Jesus even when it costs me socially or materially?
How can I ground my courage in Christ’s victory (“the blood of the Lamb”) when I feel accused or discouraged?
Where might God be providing a “wilderness” of protection or sustenance in seasons of pressure, and how can I receive it?
In what ways can my community support those facing persecution or marginalization for keeping God’s commandments?
How do I resist the pull of fear when opposition seems intense but the text insists the enemy’s time is short?
uncertainAreas: The identity of the woman (Israel, the faithful community, Mary, or a composite symbol) is debated; the text supports multiple layers. The chronology—how the child’s catching up, the heavenly war, and the earthly persecution interrelate temporally—is not explicit. The 1,260 days/“time, times, and half a time” may be symbolic or literal. The nature of the flood and the earth’s aid are figurative images whose specific historical referents are unclear.
